posts.title: A railway project is never just about the railway.
posts.text: Tanzania has secured $1.2 billion in commercial financing for the Tabora to Kigoma section of its Standard Gauge Railway. The 411 km line will connect western production areas to the wider rail network and Dar es Salaam, while improving links toward the DRC and Burundi. What interests us is what can grow around infrastructure like this.

posts.title: Sometimes entering a new market doesn’t mean doing everything alone.
posts.text: A joint venture can bring together capital, local knowledge, distribution and operating experience, but the relationship needs to be clear before the opportunity gets exciting. Who would matter more to you in a new market: a capital partner or an operating partner?

posts.title: Africa has no shortage of capital. The harder question is how easily Africans can invest across African markets.
posts.text: Dangote has been exploring ways to give investors outside Nigeria greater access to its $1.6 billion refinery IPO. Demand has already been strong, but different listing rules and regulatory requirements across African exchanges still make cross border participation more complicated.

posts.title: An existing business may already have the product and the demand.
posts.text: What limits growth can be far more practical, unreliable transport, insufficient equipment, inventory constraints or another operational bottleneck. For diaspora investors, identifying and solving that constraint can sometimes create more value than starting another company from zero. What bottleneck do you see most often in growing African SMEs?

posts.title: Some of the most interesting business relationships are forming outside the routes everyone has watched for decades.
posts.text: The companies that understand those connections early may have an advantage. Which region do you think will shape Africa’s next decade of investment most?

posts.title: Capital does not become regional just because the opportunity is regional.
posts.text: Nigeria is proposing reforms aimed at making cross border bond trading easier across West Africa. The goal is to encourage more regional investment and unlock longer term financing for infrastructure and economic growth. The interesting part is what happens if capital can move across borders with less friction.

posts.title: A growing business can have customers and still be unable to scale.
posts.text: What operational bottleneck do you see most often in growing businesses?

posts.title: Which African market would you feel most confident investing in today?
posts.text: South Africa, Mauritius, Namibia, Uganda and Kenya lead the 2026 Absa Africa Financial Markets Index. 21 of 29 markets improved their scores this year. What matters most to you when choosing a market: access, regulation or capital?

posts.title: Our new website is live!
posts.text: As part of our anniversary milestone, we've been working on making NYLE better, including how we connect with the people and businesses we serve. Our refreshed website makes it easier to learn about our work, explore our services, and understand how we support entrepreneurs, investors, and businesses across Africa.

posts.title: Private capital usually follows when the rules make room for it.
posts.text: The African Development Bank has approved $503.75 million for South Africa to support reforms across electricity, freight transport and water. The programme includes a more open electricity market, greater private participation in rail and ports and changes intended to improve infrastructure services. Infrastructure investment is not only about building more assets.

posts.title: A strong market can attract attention.
posts.text: A strong operator is what makes us keep looking. Plans change. Costs move. Customers behave differently than expected. The person running the business still has to make decisions when that happens. When you look at an opportunity, what do you judge first? The numbers or the person behind them?
